subtopics.title: Report basics and International Day of Happiness
subtopics.summary: The World Happiness Report is published annually by the Wellbeing Research Centre at the University of Oxford, in collaboration with Gallup and the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. Participants rate their lives on a scale of 0 to 10, and the report uses six key indicators. The 2026 edition was released on the International Day of Happiness, which is observed on 20 March and coincides with the vernal equinox.
facts: 2026 is the 14th edition of the World Happiness Report
Published annually since 2012
Published by the Wellbeing Research Centre, University of Oxford
Prepared in collaboration with Gallup and UN SDSN
Participants rate their lives on a scale of 0 to 10
Six key indicators: GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity, perception of corruption
Report helps countries assess development beyond GDP
International Day of Happiness observed on 20 March
Day coincides with the vernal equinox
Theme of International Day of Happiness 2026: Care and Share
Day was pioneered by Bhutan, which prioritised Gross National Happiness over GDP

subtopics.title: Global rankings 2026
subtopics.summary: Finland ranked first in the 2026 report, its ninth consecutive year at the top, with Iceland and Denmark following. Costa Rica rose to 4th place from 23rd, while Afghanistan ranked lowest at 147th. No Anglosphere nation appeared in the top 10 for a second consecutive year, which the report links to a shift in global happiness rankings.

subtopics.title: India and BRICS comparison
subtopics.summary: India ranked 116th in the 2026 report with a score of 4.536, improved from 118th. Its areas of improvement were social support and healthy life expectancy. Among BRICS nations, China ranked highest at 65th, and India ranked below Nepal and Pakistan but above Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

subtopics.title: Social media and youth well-being
subtopics.summary: The 2026 report examines how social media use relates to happiness among young people. Youth aged 15 to 24 report lower life satisfaction than those aged 60 and above, a pattern seen in the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Adolescent girls using social media for more than five hours a day are the most vulnerable group, while youth using it for under one hour a day report the best well-being.
facts: Youth aged 15-24 report lower life satisfaction than elderly aged 60+
Age-based pattern observed in US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand
Most vulnerable group: adolescent girls using social media over 5 hours a day
Heavy use linked with decline in mental health and comparison-driven stress
Optimal threshold: youth using social media under 1 hour a day
Youth using under 1 hour a day report even better well-being than non-users
Digital paradox: in developing countries like India, digital access improves education and connectivity
Excessive use in the same settings causes stress and anxiety
Report provides insights into mental health and digital behaviour trends

quizzes.passage:
Happiness is increasingly discussed as a measure of progress, not only as a private feeling. Every year, a global report asks people to rate their own lives on a scale from zero to ten and compares the results across countries. Governments and researchers use these results to judge development beyond the size of an economy. The report considers several factors, including income, social support, health, freedom, generosity and perceptions of corruption, which together help explain differences in how people feel about their lives.

Digital life has become a major area of study in recent editions. Researchers ask whether time spent on social media affects young people, and whether internet access brings benefits that outweigh its risks. The findings are mixed. Connectivity can support learning and communication, yet heavy use may be linked with stress and anxiety. Patterns also vary by age, so the experience of teenagers can differ sharply from that of older adults.

The wider theme is well-being as a policy goal. Supporters argue that a country's progress should be judged partly by the lives its people lead, and not only by how much they produce. Annual observances, held in March, also draw attention to this idea and to the value of social trust and good governance.

quizzes.passage:
A global happiness report places countries in a single ranking, and each new edition draws attention to where nations stand. The scores come from survey responses in which people rate their own lives on a scale from zero to ten. Because scores change from year to year, a country's position can rise or fall between editions, even when the difference looks small.

The report considers several areas, including economic output, community support, healthy life expectancy, freedom and generosity. Some countries perform strongly on one area and less well on another. Regional and group comparisons are also common. Emerging economies that form a bloc are often compared with each other, and neighbouring countries are compared to show how a nation performs within its own region. Social trust and governance quality are also highlighted as important features of a society.

Attention has also turned to young people. Findings suggest that age and digital habits are both connected with life satisfaction. Researchers caution that the link is not simple. In one setting, the same technology may help with education and connectivity, while in another it may create stress and anxiety. Patterns also vary by age group, so experiences can differ between generations. Such differences show that the picture is complex.
